title: Sexual Behaviour
summary: Sexual motivation as a primary motive, how it resembles hunger and thirst, the role of hormones, atypical sexual behaviour, forced sexual behaviour and sexually transmitted infections.

lesson.title: A motive for the species
lesson.hook: Skip a meal and you will die eventually. Skip sex and you won't. So why do psychologists list sexual motivation alongside hunger and thirst as a primary motive?

slides.heading: Survival of the species
slides.body:
Hunger and thirst are **primary motives** needed for the survival of the **individual**. **Sexual motivation** is also a primary motive, but it is essential for the survival of the **species**.

Without it, humans and animals that reproduce sexually would soon die out. It is driven by the **hypothalamus**, **external stimuli**, **learning**, **emotions** and **hormones**.

left.title: Hunger and thirst
points: Primary motives
Needed for the individual's survival
Deprivation is fatal

right.title: Sexual motivation
points: Primary motive
Needed for the species' survival
Individual can survive without it

slides.heading: Hypothalamic control
slides.body:
Like hunger and thirst, sexual motivation is controlled by the **hypothalamus**. If it is surgically destroyed in animals, sexual behaviour is **not initiated**, even with strong sexual stimuli.

One part of the hypothalamus **inhibits** sexual behaviour: destroy it in laboratory animals and they show **unrestrained** sexual activity. The hypothalamus also influences female sexuality indirectly through the **menstrual cycle**.

slides.question: Destroying the part of the hypothalamus that inhibits sexual behaviour in laboratory animals leads to:
slides.why: Removing the brake produces excessive sexual behaviour; destroying the initiating areas abolishes it.

slides.heading: External stimuli
slides.body:
Just as the sight and smell of food can trigger hunger, sexual motivation is highly sensitive to **external stimuli**: an attractive partner, romantic fantasies, images.

The **Coolidge effect**, seen in many animal species, is renewed sexual interest after mating when a **new** receptive partner is introduced, showing how novelty acts as a stimulus. (Some course notes describe it with the same partner; the standard definition involves a new one.)

slides.heading: Learning and emotion
slides.body:
**Learning** shapes sexuality: the huge variety of sexual behaviour within and between societies, across history, shows culture and experience at work.

**Emotions** matter too. **Stress, anxiety and depression** bring **sympathetic** arousal, while sexual arousal depends on **parasympathetic** activity, which opposes it. So these emotions usually **reduce** sexual motivation, though anxiety or depression occasionally increase it.

slides.question: Stress usually reduces sexual motivation because:
options: Sympathetic arousal opposes the parasympathetic activity that sexual arousal needs
slides.why: Sexual arousal relies on parasympathetic activity, which stress-driven sympathetic arousal works against.

slides.heading: Hormones
slides.body:
In many animals, **hormones** strongly regulate sexual motivation. Female cats, dogs and rats are receptive mainly when **ovulating** ('in heat'). **Males** are generally less tied to hormonal cycles.

In humans, hormones and sexuality are linked but less rigidly. Brecher and Brecher (1979) found that men's **testosterone** levels rose significantly while they were sexually aroused.

slides.heading: Exam season
slides.story: During final exams, a married postgraduate student notices his interest in intimacy has almost vanished. After the exams, with rest and less worry, it returns. His doctor explains that prolonged stress keeps the body in 'fight or flight' mode, which works against sexual arousal.
slides.takeaway: Emotional states such as stress shift autonomic balance and usually lower sexual motivation.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'state the similarities between sexual motivation and other primary motives'. List the four: hypothalamic control, external stimuli, learning, emotion; then add hormones. The key difference: hunger and thirst serve the individual, sex serves the species. Trap: confusing which nervous system branch supports sexual arousal (parasympathetic).
slides.sampleQuestion: Which of the following is NOT a way sexual motivation resembles hunger and thirst? (a) hypothalamic control (b) sensitivity to external stimuli (c) influence of learning (d) necessity for the individual's survival
slides.howToAnswer: Answer (d): sex is necessary for the species, not the individual. Then explain the four real similarities.

points: Sexual motivation is a primary motive for the survival of the species.
Like hunger: hypothalamic control, external stimuli, learning, emotion.
The hypothalamus both starts and inhibits sexual behaviour.
Stress (sympathetic) opposes sexual arousal (parasympathetic).
Hormones strongly drive animals; in humans testosterone rises with arousal.

questions.stem: Sexual motivation is essential mainly for the survival of the:
questions.explanation: Hunger and thirst keep the individual alive; sex keeps the species going.

questions.stem: Which brain structure controls sexual motivation as well as hunger and thirst?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus regulates these primary motives.

questions.stem: Sexual arousal is mainly mediated by which branch of the autonomic nervous system?
questions.explanation: Parasympathetic activity supports arousal; sympathetic activity opposes it.

questions.stem: Surgically destroying the hypothalamic areas that initiate sexual behaviour in animals results in:
options: No initiation of sexual behaviour even with stimuli
questions.explanation: Without these areas, sexual behaviour does not begin.

questions.stem: Female cats, dogs and rats are most sexually receptive when:
questions.explanation: Hormonal cycles tied to ovulation control receptivity in these animals.

questions.stem: Brecher and Brecher (1979) found that when men viewed erotic films, their:
questions.explanation: Sexual arousal was accompanied by higher testosterone.

questions.stem: Sexual practices vary widely between Nigerian cultures and across eras. This mainly shows the role of:
questions.explanation: Cultural and historical variety points to learning and experience.

questions.stem: A man who has lost interest in sex during months of job insecurity regains it after finding work. The best explanation is:
options: Stress-related sympathetic arousal reduced sexual motivation
questions.explanation: Chronic stress opposes the parasympathetic state needed for arousal.

questions.stem: In many animal species, a male's sexual interest returns after mating when a new receptive female is introduced. This is called the:
questions.explanation: The Coolidge effect describes renewed interest triggered by a novel partner.

questions.stem: All of the following are similarities between sexual motivation and hunger EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Unlike hunger, sex is not needed for the individual to survive.

questions.stem: Compared with females in many animal species, males' sexual behaviour is:
questions.explanation: Male animals are generally less bound to cyclical hormonal changes.

questions.stem: The hypothalamus influences female sexuality indirectly through:
questions.explanation: Its control of reproductive hormones shapes the menstrual cycle.

questions.stem: I. The hypothalamus contains areas that both initiate and inhibit sexual behaviour. II. Anxiety always reduces sexual motivation. III. Human sexuality is shaped by learning as well as biology. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Anxiety usually reduces motivation but sometimes increases it, so 'always' is wrong.

questions.stem: Why is the human link between hormones and sexual behaviour described as less rigid than in many animals?
options: Humans are only driven by hormones
Learning, emotion and culture strongly shape human sexuality alongside hormones
questions.explanation: Hormones matter in humans, but cognition, learning and culture play much larger roles.

questions.stem: A researcher lesions an animal's hypothalamus and finds it eats normally but shows no sexual behaviour. This most directly supports:
options: Separate hypothalamic areas control different primary motives
questions.explanation: Different hypothalamic regions can be damaged selectively, affecting one motive but not another.

lesson.title: Variation, harm and consent
lesson.hook: Where should psychology draw the line between sexual behaviour that is simply unusual and behaviour that is harmful? The answer turns on two words: distress and consent.

slides.heading: Unusual is not the same as abnormal
slides.body:
People differ widely in sexual preferences and practices. Your course treats many practices as **abnormal only if** the people involved find them distressing or abnormal **for themselves**.

Modern clinical practice (DSM-5) makes a similar distinction: an unusual interest becomes a **disorder** only when it causes **distress** or **harm**, or involves people who have **not consented**.

terms.meaning: Dressing in clothes of the other sex, often for arousal or to escape gender stereotypes
Arousal mainly or only from specific objects, such as shoes or underwear
Pleasure from inflicting (sadism) or receiving (masochism) pain, usually with consenting partners
Arousal from secretly watching unaware people undress or have sex
Arousal from exposing one's genitals to unsuspecting others

slides.heading: Transsexualism and gender dysphoria
slides.body:
Your course describes **transsexualism** as feeling **trapped in a body of the wrong sex**: for example, someone anatomically male who feels he is a woman. Unlike transvestism, cross-dressing here is **not about arousal**; the person feels they are wearing the clothes of their **true sex**. Some undergo hormone treatment or surgery.

Today's clinical term is **gender dysphoria**, which focuses on the **distress** caused by the mismatch.

slides.question: What mainly distinguishes transsexualism from transvestism, as described in the course?
options: For transsexuals, cross-dressing reflects felt gender, not sexual arousal
Transvestites feel trapped in the wrong body
slides.why: Transvestism is often linked to arousal; transsexualism concerns feeling one's true sex differs from one's body.

slides.heading: Why voyeurism and exhibitionism are abnormal
slides.body:
**Voyeurs** are aroused only when those watched are **unaware**, often with an element of **danger**. They are usually males who struggle to form normal sexual relationships. **Exhibitionists**, often shy men with inhibited sex lives, want to **shock** but are rarely dangerous.

Both are treated as abnormal because they **frighten victims** who have **not consented**, and both are **illegal**.

slides.heading: Forced sexual behaviour
slides.body:
**Forced sexual behaviour** involves **actual, threatened or implied force** against a victim. It includes **rape**, **sexual abuse of children**, **incest** and **sexual harassment**.

After **rape**, victims often feel their whole life has changed, with intense **anxiety**, **depression**, and disturbed **sleep, relationships** and daily functioning. Most rapists are male and most victims female, though not always.

left.title: Defined by relationship
points: Incest: abuser is a family member
Most abusers know the child
Often neighbours or relatives

right.title: Defined by force
points: Child rape: force or threat used
Child molestation: no force
Abusers often win trust first

slides.heading: Sexual harassment
slides.body:
**Sexual harassment** includes **sexual approaches the person does not want**, **demands for sex in exchange for favours** (such as grades or jobs), and **touching without consent**. It usually happens between people with **unequal power**, such as lecturer and student, or boss and worker.

Because of that power gap, most cases **go unreported**. Victims become uneasy at school or work and may develop serious **anxiety and depression**. In Nigeria, the VAPP Act (2015) and university policies provide routes to report it.

slides.heading: Speaking up
slides.story: A 200-level student, Ruth, is told by a course adviser that her missing result can be 'sorted' if she visits his house. She refuses, saves the messages and reports to the university's gender desk with a friend. The investigation finds other students had faced the same demand but stayed silent, fearing their grades.
slides.takeaway: Power imbalance keeps most harassment hidden; evidence, support and formal reporting channels help victims come forward.

slides.question: Most incidents of sexual harassment go unreported mainly because of:
options: The power imbalance between harasser and victim
slides.why: Victims fear consequences from someone with power over their grades, job or safety.

slides.heading: Sexually transmitted infections
slides.body:
**Sexually transmitted infections (STIs)** are caused by micro-organisms spread through sexual contact. Common ones include **syphilis, gonorrhoea, chlamydia, genital herpes, genital warts** and **HIV**, which can lead to **AIDS**.

Some are easily cured if caught early; others are incurable. Untreated STIs can cause **infertility** and endanger **pregnant women and babies**. Risk rises sharply with **unsafe sex**, so all STIs need prompt medical care.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect 'explain five forms of unusual sexual behaviour' and 'when does sexual behaviour become forced?'. Define each clearly and give the key feature: objects (fetishism), pain (sadism/masochism), unaware targets (voyeurism), exposing (exhibitionism). Forced behaviour always turns on consent. Use clinical language in answers.
slides.sampleQuestion: Mention three forms of forced sexual behaviour and explain when sexual behaviour becomes forced.
slides.howToAnswer: Name rape, child sexual abuse (including incest) and sexual harassment. Explain that behaviour is forced when it involves actual, threatened or implied force, or lacks the victim's consent, and note the psychological effects.

points: Unusual practices become disorders when they cause distress, harm or lack consent.
Atypical: transvestism, fetishism, sadism/masochism, voyeurism, exhibitionism.
Transsexualism, now gender dysphoria, concerns felt gender, not arousal.
Forced: rape, child sexual abuse, incest, harassment; consent is the key.
STIs: some curable, some not; untreated, they threaten fertility and babies.

questions.stem: Sexual arousal mainly from specific objects such as shoes is called:
questions.explanation: Fetishism centres arousal on objects.

questions.stem: Gaining sexual pleasure from secretly watching unaware people undress is:
questions.explanation: Voyeurism involves watching people who do not know they are observed.

questions.stem: Sexual abuse of a child by a family member is termed:
questions.explanation: Incest is sexual contact by a family member.

questions.stem: Sexual masochism refers to:
questions.explanation: Masochism is arousal from receiving pain; sadism is from inflicting it.

questions.stem: Sexual harassment most often occurs between people who:
questions.explanation: Power imbalance, at school or work, is typical.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a sexually transmitted infection?
questions.explanation: Gonorrhoea spreads through sexual contact.

questions.stem: A man repeatedly exposes his genitals to women at a bus stop to shock them. This is:
questions.explanation: Exposing oneself to unsuspecting others is exhibitionism.

questions.stem: A lecturer hints that a student's grade depends on a 'favour' and touches her without consent. This is:
questions.explanation: Unwanted advances and touching by someone with power is harassment.

questions.stem: An adult abuses a child without using force, after first gaining the child's trust. This is best termed:
questions.explanation: Abuse without force or threat of force is described as child molestation; with force it is child rape.

questions.stem: Which feature makes voyeurism abnormal in the course's view?
options: It frightens unaware victims and is illegal
questions.explanation: Lack of consent, fear caused to victims and illegality mark it as abnormal.

questions.stem: All of the following are forms of forced sexual behaviour EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Consensual adult practices do not involve force.

questions.stem: Why are child abusers often hard to detect?
options: They are often known to the child and first gain trust
questions.explanation: Most abusers are neighbours or relatives who build trust before abusing.

questions.stem: I. Untreated STIs can cause infertility. II. All STIs are easily curable. III. Risk of STIs rises with unsafe sex. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. Some STIs, such as HIV, are incurable.

questions.stem: What single principle best separates acceptable sexual variation from forced sexual behaviour?
questions.explanation: Forced behaviour lacks consent and involves actual, threatened or implied force.

questions.stem: A rape survivor reports months of sleeplessness, fear and withdrawal from friends. These reactions are best described as:
options: Unusual and unrelated to the assault
questions.explanation: Anxiety, depression, sleep and relationship problems commonly follow rape.
